title: Postgres jsonb: The Field Handbook
summary: A dense, example-driven tour of Postgres jsonb — how it is stored, every operator you need, containment and existence semantics, SQL/JSON path queries, GIN and expression indexing, and the trade-offs that decide when a real column beats a document.

chapters.title: json vs jsonb: What Postgres Actually Stores
points: Two types, one syntax: `json` and `jsonb` both accept RFC 8259 text, but store it completely differently.
`json` keeps an exact text copy: whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys all survive verbatim; every read re-parses the string.
`jsonb` stores a decomposed binary tree: parsed once on input, no reparse on read, so operators and indexes are fast.
jsonb normalizes on the way in: whitespace stripped, duplicate keys collapsed (last one wins), object keys reordered.
jsonb key order is not insertion order and not alphabetical — keys sort by length first, then bytewise: `{"z":1,"aa":2}` prints `{"z": 1, "aa": 2}`.
jsonb numbers are stored as `numeric`: exact decimal, no float artifacts — but `NaN` and `Infinity` are rejected because numeric-in-JSON has no syntax for them.
Neither type accepts `\u0000` in strings; the server encoding must also be able to represent any `\uXXXX` escape.
jsonb has a total order and equality, so `=`, `<`, `DISTINCT`, `GROUP BY`, and btree indexes on the whole value work. `json` has none of that — `SELECT DISTINCT json_col` is an error.
jsonb comparison order across types: Object > Array > Boolean > Number > String > Null; objects compare by key count first, then key/value pairs.
Size cap: a jsonb value tops out around 255 MB (internal offsets); `json`, being just text, goes to 1 GB.
Write cost: jsonb pays parse + build at INSERT; `json` pays nothing at write and everything at every read.
Choose `json` only when you must round-trip the byte-exact payload — webhook signature verification, audit logs of raw bodies, key-order-sensitive clients.
Choose `jsonb` for everything you intend to query, index, or mutate — which is nearly everything.
Rule of thumb: `json` is a text column with a validator; `jsonb` is a data structure.

chapters.title: Creating, Casting, and Inspecting jsonb
points: Literal + cast is the base case: `SELECT '{"a":1,"tags":["x"]}'::jsonb;` — malformed text raises `invalid input syntax for type json` with a byte position.
`to_jsonb(anyelement)` converts any SQL value, including composites and arrays: `to_jsonb(ROW(1,'x'))`, `to_jsonb(ARRAY[1,2,3])`.
`jsonb_build_object('id', 1, 'ok', true)` — variadic key/value pairs, keeps SQL types; safer than string concatenation, which is a JSON-injection bug waiting to happen.
`jsonb_build_array(1, 'two', null)` builds heterogeneous arrays.
`row_to_json(t)` / `to_jsonb(t)` over a table alias turns a whole row into a document with column names as keys.
`jsonb_typeof(v)` returns one of `object`, `array`, `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null` — the only reliable way to branch on shape.
SQL NULL is not JSON null: `NULL::jsonb IS NULL` is true; `'null'::jsonb IS NULL` is false. `jsonb_typeof('null'::jsonb)` = `'null'`.
`jsonb_array_length(v)` errors if `v` is not an array — guard it with `jsonb_typeof(v) = 'array'`.
`jsonb_object_keys(v)` is set-returning: one row per top-level key, objects only.
`jsonb_pretty(v)` reformats with indentation for humans; never store the pretty form, jsonb normalizes it away anyway.
`jsonb_object(ARRAY['a','1','b','2'])` builds from a flat text array; the two-array form `jsonb_object(keys, values)` is often cleaner.
Casting out: `v::text` renders canonical JSON text; `v #>> '{}'` extracts a scalar's text without the surrounding quotes.
Validate before you trust: a `CHECK (jsonb_typeof(data) = 'object')` constraint stops scalars and arrays sneaking into a column meant for records.
`jsonb_strip_nulls(v)` drops object fields whose value is JSON null — useful to shrink sparse documents at write time (it leaves nulls inside arrays alone).

chapters.title: Extraction: ->, ->>, #>, #>> and Subscripting
points: `->` returns jsonb: `data -> 'user'` gives a document you can keep chaining.
`->>` returns text: `data ->> 'name'` gives `Ada`, not `"Ada"` — the quotes are gone and so is the type.
Same operators on arrays with an integer: `data -> 'tags' -> 0`, and negative indexes count from the end: `-> -1` is the last element.
Chain rule: use `->` for every step except the last, then `->>` — `data -> 'user' -> 'addr' ->> 'city'`.
`#>` and `#>>` take a text[] path and do it in one hop: `data #>> '{user,addr,city}'`, array indexes written as digits: `'{items,0,sku}'`.
Missing key returns SQL NULL, never an error — so typos fail silently. `data ->> 'nmae'` is just NULL.
Ambiguity trap: `data ->> 'k'` returns NULL both when the key is absent and when its value is JSON null. Use `data ? 'k'` or `jsonb_typeof(data->'k')` to tell them apart.
`->>` output is `text`, so comparisons are string comparisons: `'10' < '9'` is true. Cast for numbers: `(data->>'qty')::int > 9`.
Casting is a runtime landmine: one row with `"qty": "n/a"` and the whole query dies with `invalid input syntax for type integer`.
Subscripting (PG 14+) reads like an array: `data['user']['city']` — equivalent to `->`, returns jsonb, and integer subscripts index arrays.
Subscripts also assign: `UPDATE t SET data['status'] = '"done"'::jsonb;` — the value must be jsonb, so scalars need quotes and a cast.
Subscript assignment creates missing keys and pads arrays with nulls when the index is past the end.
`->` on the wrong shape is quiet: integer subscript on an object or text key on an array yields NULL, not an error.
None of these operators are GIN-indexable on their own — `data->>'x' = 'y'` needs an expression index or a rewrite to `@>` (see Ch. 8-9).

chapters.title: Containment and Existence: @>, <@, ?, ?|, ?&
points: `@>` asks 'is the right side contained in the left side?' — the workhorse operator, and the one GIN indexes best.
Object containment is subset-of-pairs: `'{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb @> '{"a":1}'` is true.
Nesting is structural, not flattened: `'{"a":{"b":1,"c":2}}' @> '{"a":{"b":1}}'` is true; `@> '{"b":1}'` is false.
Array containment ignores order and duplicates: `'[1,2,3]' @> '[3,1]'` is true, `'[1,2,3]' @> '[1,1]'` is also true.
Special top-level exception: a bare scalar is contained in an array — `'["a","b"]'::jsonb @> '"b"'` is true.
That exception does not apply at depth: `'{"t":[1,2,3]}' @> '{"t":3}'` is FALSE; you must write `@> '{"t":[3]}'`.
Everything contains the empty structure: `'{"a":1}' @> '{}'` and `'[1,2]' @> '[]'` are both true — a fine no-op filter, a useless index probe.
`<@` is `@>` with operands swapped: `'{"a":1}' <@ '{"a":1,"b":2}'`.
`?` is key/element existence and only ever matches strings: object keys, array string elements, or a top-level string scalar. `'{"a":1}' ? 'a'` true; `'[1,2]' ? '1'` false.
`?` does not look at values: `'{"a":"x"}' ? 'x'` is false. It is not a substring search.
`?|` = any of, `?&` = all of, both take a `text[]`: `data ?& array['name','email']`.
Existence is top-level only — no recursive descent. For deep checks use `#>` plus `?`, or jsonpath `@?`.
Idiom: filter a tag array with `data @> '{"tags":["sql"]}'` — index-friendly, order-agnostic, and it survives the array growing.
Idiom: a multi-key equality filter is one containment probe — `data @> '{"status":"open","team":"core"}'` beats three `->>` comparisons.
Gotcha: `@>` matches values by exact JSON type, so `@> '{"qty":5}'` will not match a document storing `"qty": "5"`.

chapters.title: Mutating Documents: ||, -, #-, jsonb_set
points: jsonb values are immutable — every 'mutation' function returns a new document; there is no in-place patch.
`||` concatenates: on two objects it is a SHALLOW merge, right side wins on key conflicts — `'{"a":{"x":1}}' || '{"a":{"y":2}}'` yields `{"a":{"y":2}}`, the `x` is gone.
There is no built-in deep merge; write a recursive SQL/PLpgSQL function or merge leaf paths explicitly.
`||` on two arrays concatenates them; on a non-array plus anything it builds an array: `'1'::jsonb || '2'::jsonb` = `[1, 2]`.
`- 'key'` removes a top-level object key; `- 2` removes an array element by index (negatives count from the end); `- array['a','b']` removes several keys at once.
`#- '{a,b}'` deletes at a path, object key or array index alike.
`jsonb_set(target, path text[], new_value jsonb [, create_missing boolean DEFAULT true])` replaces a value at a path.
Example: `jsonb_set(data, '{addr,city}', '"Cork"')` — note the inner quotes; the new value must be valid jsonb, so plain `'Cork'` is a syntax error.
With `create_missing = false`, a path that does not exist leaves the document untouched instead of adding the key.

The NULL trap: if any argument is SQL NULL, `jsonb_set` returns NULL and your UPDATE wipes the whole column. Guard with `coalesce(...)` or use `jsonb_set_lax(..., null_value_treatment => 'use_json_null' | 'delete_key' | 'return_target' | 'raise_exception')`.
`jsonb_insert(target, path, new_value [, insert_after])` adds without overwriting — it errors if the target already exists, and inserts into arrays at a position.

Update cost is the real story: `UPDATE t SET data = jsonb_set(data, ...)` rewrites the entire row under MVCC, re-TOASTs the whole document, and touches every index on the table unless the update qualifies as HOT.
So a 40 KB document with a hit counter is a bad design: each increment writes 40 KB of new tuple plus WAL. Move the counter to its own column.

Concurrency: two sessions read-modify-writing the same document produce last-writer-wins loss. Serialize with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or do the mutation in a single statement so the row lock covers it.
`jsonb_strip_nulls` after a merge cleans up keys explicitly set to null by the incoming patch.

chapters.title: Documents to Rows and Back: Unnest and Aggregate
points: `jsonb_each(v)` returns `(key text, value jsonb)`; `jsonb_each_text(v)` returns the value as text. Objects only.
`jsonb_array_elements(v)` returns one jsonb row per array element; `jsonb_array_elements_text(v)` unquotes them.
Put set-returning functions in `FROM` with `LATERAL`, not in the SELECT list: `FROM t, LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(t.data->'items') AS e(item)`.
`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` drops rows with an empty or missing array; use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` to keep them.
`jsonb_to_record(v) AS x(id int, name text)` shreds a flat document into typed columns — the `AS` column list is mandatory because the type is only known at parse time.
`jsonb_to_recordset(v) AS x(sku text, qty int)` does the same for an array of objects — the standard way to bulk-load a JSON payload into relational form.
`jsonb_populate_record(null::my_type, v)` uses an existing composite type or table rowtype instead of an inline column list; `jsonb_populate_recordset` for arrays.
Going the other way: `jsonb_agg(expr)` collects rows into a JSON array, `jsonb_object_agg(k, v)` collects them into an object.
`jsonb_agg` over an empty group returns NULL, not `[]` — wrap it: `coalesce(jsonb_agg(x), '[]'::jsonb)`.
Order inside an aggregate is explicit: `jsonb_agg(item ORDER BY item->>'sku')`; without it the array order is whatever the plan produced.
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` composes with these: `jsonb_agg(item) FILTER (WHERE item->>'state' = 'ok')`.
Build a nested API response in one query with a correlated subquery: `SELECT to_jsonb(o) || jsonb_build_object('lines', (SELECT jsonb_agg(l) FROM lines l WHERE l.order_id = o.id)) FROM orders o`.
Aggregation is the performance cliff: unnesting a million documents to filter them scans everything. Filter with `@>` or jsonpath FIRST so an index cuts the row set, then unnest the survivors.
`jsonb_path_query` (Ch. 7) often replaces a chain of nested `jsonb_array_elements` calls with a single expression.

chapters.title: SQL/JSON Path Queries: jsonpath, @?, @@
points: `jsonpath` is a real type with its own mini-language, added in PG 12 — think XPath for JSON.
Basics: `$` is the root document, `$.a.b` navigates keys, `$.items[0]` indexes, `$.items[*]` iterates, `$.items[1 to 3]` slices, `$.*` takes all values.
`.**` is recursive descent: `$.**.id` finds every `id` at any depth; `$.**{2}` limits the level count.
Filters use `?()` with `@` as the current item: `$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 10)`.
Filter predicates: `== != < <= > >=`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `exists(...)`, `like_regex "^a" flag "i"`, `starts with "pre"`, `is unknown`.
Item methods: `.type()`, `.size()`, `.double()`, `.abs()`, `.floor()`, `.ceiling()`, `.keyvalue()`, `.datetime(template)`.
Lax mode (the default) auto-unwraps arrays and swallows missing/structural errors as 'no match'; `strict` mode refuses to unwrap and raises errors instead. Prefix the path with `strict` to opt in.
Lax unwrapping is why `$.tags ? (@ == "sql")` works whether `tags` is a string or an array of strings — convenient, and occasionally a lie.
`@?` tests 'does this path return at least one item': `data @? '$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 10)'`.
`@@` evaluates a path that IS a predicate and returns its boolean: `data @@ '$.qty > 10'`. Mixing the two up is the classic beginner error — `@?` takes a locator, `@@` takes a predicate.
Function forms mirror the operators: `jsonb_path_exists`, `jsonb_path_match`, `jsonb_path_query` (set-returning), `jsonb_path_query_first`, `jsonb_path_query_array`.
Pass parameters safely with the `vars` argument instead of building path strings: `jsonb_path_query(data, '$.items[*] ? (@.sku == $s)', '{"s":"A1"}')`.
The fourth `silent` argument suppresses structural errors from strict mode, mimicking lax behaviour per-call.
PG 17 adds SQL-standard `JSON_EXISTS`, `JSON_VALUE`, `JSON_QUERY`, and `JSON_TABLE(...COLUMNS(...))`, which turns a document into a relation in one clause.

Indexing caveat: GIN can only accelerate `@?`/`@@` for the restricted shapes it can reduce to containment — plain key accessors with `==` equality. Ranges, regex, and `.**` fall back to a full scan of the candidate set.

chapters.title: GIN Indexing: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
points: GIN is an inverted index: it maps each extracted key to the list of rows containing it — the right structure for 'which documents contain this bit'.
Default opclass `jsonb_ops`: indexes every key AND every value as separate entries, keys included as their own strings.
`jsonb_ops` supports `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?`, `@@` — it is the only choice if you need key-existence queries.
`jsonb_path_ops`: `CREATE INDEX ON t USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops);` stores a single hash per full path-to-value, and nothing for keys alone.
`jsonb_path_ops` supports only `@>`, `@?`, `@@`. `data ? 'k'` cannot use it.
Trade: `jsonb_path_ops` is typically much smaller and faster for containment, because one hash entry replaces several key/value entries and there is no giant posting list for a common key name.

Why the common key hurts `jsonb_ops`: a key present in every row has a posting list of every row, so `@> '{"status":"open"}'` scans two huge lists and intersects them. `jsonb_path_ops` probes one selective hash.

Both are lossy: GIN stores no reconstructable value, so every match is rechecked against the heap tuple. Expect `Bitmap Index Scan` + `Bitmap Heap Scan` with `Recheck Cond`, and never an index-only scan.
Hash collisions in `jsonb_path_ops` produce false positives, which the recheck filters out — correct results, slightly more heap work.
Index the smallest useful expression: `USING gin ((data -> 'tags'))` indexes only the tags subtree, giving a fraction of the size, then query `data -> 'tags' @> '["sql"]'`.
The indexed expression must appear verbatim in the query for the planner to use it — `data->'tags' @> ...` will not match an index built on `data`.
Partial GIN for a hot subset: `CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops) WHERE tenant_id = 42;` or `WHERE data ? 'archived_at'`.

Write cost: GIN inserts are expensive; `fastupdate = on` (default) buffers them in a pending list flushed by VACUUM or when `gin_pending_list_limit` is hit — fast writes, but a query may have to scan the pending list, causing latency spikes.
Set `fastupdate = off` for read-latency-sensitive tables; keep it on for write-heavy bulk ingestion.
Bulk-load pattern: drop the GIN index, COPY the data, rebuild — far cheaper than maintaining it row by row. Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the rebuild.
`btree_gin` extension lets you put a scalar column and jsonb in one GIN index: `USING gin (tenant_id, data jsonb_path_ops)`.

chapters.title: Expression Indexes, TOAST, and the Planner
points: GIN cannot help range, sort, or unique constraints. For those, index the extracted scalar with btree: `CREATE INDEX ON t ((data ->> 'email'));`
Typed version needs the cast inside the index and in the query: `CREATE INDEX ON t (((data ->> 'age')::int));` then `WHERE (data->>'age')::int > 30`.
The cast must be IMMUTABLE — `::timestamptz` from text is not, so store UTC and cast to `timestamp` instead, or use a stable helper.
Uniqueness inside a document is possible: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON t ((data ->> 'email'));` — one of the few real constraints jsonb can carry.

The generated-column pattern (PG 12+) is usually better than an expression index: `email text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (data ->> 'email') STORED` — then index it, add NOT NULL, add a CHECK, reference it from views.
Rule: keep the document as the source of truth, promote hot keys to generated columns as the query patterns reveal themselves.
TOAST: a row wider than ~2 KB pushes the jsonb value out of line and compresses it. Reading a single key detoasts and decompresses the WHOLE document — there is no partial read of a jsonb field.
So `SELECT data->>'id'` on a 200 KB document does 200 KB of work per row. Narrow, frequently-read fields belong in columns, not deep in a fat document.
`ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN data SET STORAGE EXTERNAL` skips compression: bigger on disk, cheaper CPU per read. Measure before adopting.
Planner blindness: Postgres collects no per-key statistics for jsonb, so `@>` selectivity is a fixed guess (roughly 0.1%) regardless of how common the value is.
The consequence is bad plans at scale — a wildly wrong row estimate feeds the wrong join order or a nested loop over a million rows. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and compare estimated vs actual rows.
A generated column gets real statistics — histograms, MCVs, n_distinct — which is often the actual reason the query gets faster, not the index.
Storage overhead: every row repeats every key name. A million rows with a `"description"` key pay for that string a million times; a column stores the name once in the catalog.

Rough cost model: GIN containment probe is O(entries in the query) list intersections plus a heap recheck per candidate; btree on a generated column is O(log n) with no recheck. Prefer btree when the key is always present.
Trigram option for text search inside a field: `CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm; CREATE INDEX ON t USING gin ((data ->> 'title') gin_trgm_ops);` to make `LIKE '%foo%'` indexable.

chapters.title: When a Column Beats a Document (and the Mistakes to Avoid)
points: Use a column when the field is filtered, joined, sorted, or aggregated on — you get statistics, btree indexes, and plans that do not guess.
Use a column when the field needs integrity: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, and especially FOREIGN KEY — a jsonb field can never reference another table.
Use a column when the field is updated frequently and the document is large — jsonb updates rewrite the whole row and re-TOAST the whole value.
Use jsonb when attributes are sparse, unbounded, or caller-defined: third-party webhook payloads, per-tenant custom fields, feature flags, event properties.
Use jsonb when the access pattern is whole-document read/write, or when the shape versions faster than you can ship migrations.
jsonb as an EAV replacement is a genuine win: one indexed column beats an attribute table with a self-join per attribute.
The hybrid is the mature answer: stable core as columns, variable tail as jsonb, hot jsonb keys promoted to generated columns. Postgres allows 1600 columns; a document counts as one.
Mistake: `data->>'k' = 'v'` when you meant `data @> '{"k":"v"}'` — the first cannot use a GIN index, the second can.
Mistake: comparing `->>` output numerically without a cast — text ordering says `'10' < '9'`.
Mistake: `@> '{"tags":"sql"}'` for an array field — containment needs `'{"tags":["sql"]}'`, and the top-level scalar exception does not reach nested levels.
Mistake: treating a missing key and a JSON null as the same thing because `->>` returns NULL for both.
Mistake: `jsonb_set` with a NULL argument, silently nulling the whole column in an UPDATE.
Mistake: relying on key order or duplicate keys surviving a jsonb round trip — they do not; use `json` or `text` for byte-exact payloads.
Mistake: building JSON with string concatenation instead of `jsonb_build_object`, which is a JSON-injection hole.
Mistake: one giant document per row for data you query field by field — you pay full detoast on every read.

Summary: jsonb is a parsed, ordered, indexable structure; `@>` plus GIN is the fast path; jsonpath is the expressive path; expression and generated columns supply the constraints and statistics that jsonb lacks; and the moment a key becomes load-bearing, promote it to a column.
